result: The study demonstrates that patients' colorectal tumors exhibit significantly higher metabolic heterogeneity compared to cultured cells and tumor xenografts, as measured by NAD(P)H FLIM. This heterogeneity manifests as wider and frequently bimodal distributions of the free (glycolytic) NAD(P)H fraction, with heterogeneity increasing with model complexity.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The editor states 'the indication is that the level of heterogeneity of cellular metabolism increases with model complexity and demonstrates high heterogeneity at a clinical level' and that 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid.' Reviewer 1 notes this as the 'merit of this study' and Reviewer 2 describes the experiments as 'solid' and 'well-organized.'

result: Among patient tumors, dispersion of the free NAD(P)H fraction (D-a1) was significantly associated with clinical characteristics: higher in early-stage (T1, T2) tumors compared to advanced stages (T3, T4) (p=0.02), and higher in high-grade (G3) versus low-grade tumors (p=0.04). Notably, dispersion showed no correlation with bimodality.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these associations between metabolic heterogeneity and clinical features. Reviewer 1 states the study 'find[s] that NAD(P)H fluorescence properties have a strong potential to distinguish between high- and low-grade tumors and a moderate ability to distinguish advanced stage tumors from low stage tumors.' The editor notes that additional samples from 8 patients were added during revision, which 'is helpful for the conclusions that the authors are trying to draw.'

result: The authors conclude that cell-level metabolic heterogeneity assessed from NAD(P)H FLIM has potential to become a clinical prognostic factor, based on the associations found between heterogeneity metrics and clinical tumor characteristics.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the prognostic potential while acknowledging limitations. Reviewer 1 states the study 'provides valuable results contributing to the deployment of minimally invasive optical imaging techniques to quantify tumor properties and potentially migrating into tools for human tumor characterization and clinical diagnosis.' Reviewer 2 notes 'it was shown that heterogeneity of patients' samples had associations with clinical characteristics of tumors,' though also mentions 'maybe more patients should be involved in the future for reliable diagnosis and prognosis.'

result: Cell lines showed characteristic NAD(P)H fluorescence lifetimes and distinct metabolic profiles: CT26 and HCT116 exhibited high glycolytic metabolism (high a1, low τm), while CaCo2 showed more OXPHOS-shifted metabolism (low a1, high τm). All cell lines were metabolically uniform with minor intercellular variations (<3%) and bimodality indices below 1.1.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the solid experimental foundation. The editor states 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid' and Reviewer 2 describes the experiments as 'solid' and 'well-organized, including in vitro and in vivo animal models and ex vivo patient samples.' No concerns were raised about the cell line characterization data.

result: Tumor xenografts showed increased metabolic heterogeneity compared to cell lines, with larger intercellular variations (≥3% vs ≤3%), dispersion of 2.6-4.0%, and bimodal distributions in 5 of 19 tumors. The nonuniform microenvironment was identified as a major source of this variable metabolism.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the progression from simple to complex models. Reviewer 1 notes 'the investigation of colorectal samples under multiple imaging scenarios with the same instrument and approach conforms to a valuable dataset that can facilitate interpretation of results across the spectrum of sample complexity.' No specific concerns were raised about the xenograft data.

result: Patient tumors exhibited the highest metabolic heterogeneity with NAD(P)H-a1 ranging from 62-80%, dispersion from 2.19-11.99%, and 14 of 29 tumors showing bimodal distributions (BI≥1.1). Bimodality index showed no correlation with dispersion, indicating these metrics capture different aspects of heterogeneity.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings on patient tumor heterogeneity. The editor notes 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid, and at the revision stage, the authors have included additional samples from 8 patients in the data pool, which is helpful for the conclusions.' Reviewer 2 similarly states 'additional samples from 8 patients were added to the data pool during the revision process, which is helpful and important for the conclusions that the authors are trying to draw.'

result: SHAP analysis revealed that dispersion of a1 had major relative weight in predicting clinical characteristics. Primary tumors with metastases showed a tendency toward lower D-a1 compared to tumors without metastases (p=0.056).
evaluation: Reviewers accept these analytical findings without raising concerns. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'find[s]...a moderate ability to distinguish advanced stage tumors from low stage tumors,' which aligns with the near-significant metastasis association. The SHAP analysis is not specifically critiqued by any reviewer.

result: Immunohistochemical analysis showed >90% EpCAM-positive cells in xenografts and 76±10% in patient tumors. The ratio of EpCAM to vimentin-positive cells did not correlate with metabolic heterogeneity metrics (D-a1 or BI-a1), indicating mesenchymal phenotype presence did not contribute to FLIM-detected metabolic heterogeneity.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. The immunohistochemical characterization is part of the 'solid experiments' noted by Reviewer 2. No reviewer questions the interpretation that epithelial-mesenchymal composition does not explain the observed metabolic heterogeneity.

result: The authors attempted to measure flavin fluorescence but found the signal was very low (~27 times lower than NAD(P)H) and insufficient for proper analysis.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges this limitation, stating 'NAD(P)H fluorescence provides a partial picture of the cell/tissue metabolic characteristics. Including fluorescence from flavins would comprise a more compelling dataset...The authors did attempt to incorporate flavin fluorescence, unfortunately they could not find strong enough signal to proceed with the analysis.' This shows the reviewer accepts the technical limitation.

result: The authors conclude that FLIM-microscopy provides unique subcellular resolution (~200-500 nm) information about metabolic heterogeneity unavailable with other methods, and that patient tumor metabolic landscapes are hardly reproducible in in vitro and in vivo models, highlighting the importance of clinical material investigation and the technique's potential for clinical translation.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the value and uniqueness of the approach. The editor states 'the work will be of interest to medical biologists developing methods for quantifying metabolic heterogeneity.' Reviewer 1 notes the study 'provides valuable results contributing to the deployment of minimally invasive optical imaging techniques' and that it 'can facilitate interpretation of results across the spectrum of sample complexity.' Reviewer 2 describes the work as 'logically well-designed.'
